To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

weight change and blood sugar levels before diabetes onset are potential predictors of cancer related diabetes, and may help to target subjects with new onset of diabetes for pancreatic cancer screening.
weight loss and blood glucose levels in subjects with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes are associated with an increased odds of pancreatic cancer related type 2 diabetes.
subjects with cancer related diabetes have a 3.6 times higher risk of developing pancreatic cancer than subjects with normal type 2 DM.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel approach to the early detection of pancreatic cancer.
understanding the role of the immune system in the pathogenesis of pancreatic cancer.
the development of new, more effective treatments for pancreatic cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is insufficient to determine the effect of weight change on risk of pancreatic cancer.
weight change and blood sugar levels before the onset of new diabetes can predict pancreatic cancer, and therefore, it can be used for the early detection of pancreatic cancer.

weight change and blood sugar level in the normal range before the onset of type 2 diabetes may serve as markers for pancreatic cancers and may help identify subjects who should be referred to screening examinations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have found that weight loss before the onset of new diabetes and blood glucose levels in normal range (and therefore rapid development of hypergylcemia) may be predictive of cancer related diabetes and therefore may be helpful in targeting which patients with newly diagnosed diabetes to refer for screening for pancreatic cancer.
the development of diabetes in a patient is a warning sign that something is going on with the pancreas and the patient needs to be referred for a pancreatic cancer screening examination.

weight loss and high normal blood glucose before diabetes onset are associated with an increased likelihood of cancer related diabetes, which in turn is associated with a higher risk of pancreatic cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of new onset diabetes, even in the absence of any other symptoms, is an important warning sign for pancreatic cancer.
pancreatic cancer is not the only reason for new onset diabetes.
pancreatic cancer is associated with a specific pattern of weight loss and hyperglycemia before the onset of new diabetes.
